record.paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
record.original_question: Once a variant or gene is causally linked to a human trait, how can researchers discover the biological mechanism by which it affects the trait—especially for weak-effect noncoding variants and highly polygenic or omnigenic traits—using analytical or experimental strategies despite the limited ability to run controlled organism-level experiments in humans?

evidence.quote: Even among genetic effects for which causality is established, only a small fraction have a known, well-established biological mechanism (open problem #13: from causality to mechanism).
As most causal variants are in non-coding regions and exert weak effects, it is challenging to understand how they affect traits
In light of these challenges, devising experimental and analytical strategies for finding or guiding the search for biological mechanism would be of tremendous benefit.

artifact.category_tag: human trait genetics — causality to mechanism
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broad open research question in human trait genetics. Recent reviews (2022–2025) on GWAS follow-up, variant-to-function (V2F) initiatives, and omnigenic-model studies continue to describe mechanism elucidation for noncoding, weak-effect variants in polygenic traits as an unresolved central challenge, with progress on individual loci but no general solution.

status_evidence.title: Open problems in human trait genetics (arXiv:2108.06684)

status_evidence.claim: The problem is explicitly framed as open.

status_evidence.title: NHGRI Variant-to-Function (V2F) initiative
status_evidence.snippet: Ongoing program funding methods to translate GWAS variants into mechanistic understanding, indicating the problem remains an active research frontier.
status_evidence.claim: Major funders treat the variant-to-mechanism problem as unsolved and ongoing.
